name: Hacking & attack tools
source: Flipper Devices identifiers from the bundled Bluetooth SIG (company 0x0E29) and IEEE (0C:FA:22) registries; other tools by their default advertised names / SSIDs as published by their projects and reported by the community. Owning these tools is legal and common among hobbyists — a hit means 'someone nearby has one', not that you are being attacked.

rules.label: Flipper Zero
rules.note: Flipper Devices SIG company 0x0E29 and OUI 0C:FA:22; Flipper Zero advertises 'Flipper <name>' over BLE. Multi-tool for Sub-GHz, RFID/NFC, IR, BadUSB and BLE (incl. BLE-spam firmware).

rules.label: Hak5 WiFi Pineapple (rogue access point)
rules.note: WiFi Pineapple management SSIDs ('Pineapple_XXXX', MK7). Pineapples conventionally use BSSIDs starting 00:13:37, which is officially registered to Orient Power — so the OUI alone is not used. PineAP impersonates networks your devices have joined before (see evil-twin alerts).

rules.label: ESP32 / ESP8266 attack firmware (deauther, Marauder, Bruce, Nemo, GhostESP)
rules.note: Default SSIDs / BLE names of popular Wi-Fi attack firmwares: Spacehuhn ESP8266 Deauther ('pwned'), ESP32 Marauder, Bruce, M5Stick NEMO, GhostESP, WiFi Nugget, evil-portal captive portals. These can deauthenticate Wi-Fi clients, clone networks and spam BLE.

rules.label: Pwnagotchi (Wi-Fi handshake capture)
rules.note: Pwnagotchi peers announce themselves in beacons (custom information element 222 with JSON); RFWatch also checks for that element directly. Collects WPA handshakes by deauthenticating clients.

rules.label: Covert hardware implant (O.MG cable / keylogger)
rules.note: Wi-Fi access points opened by covert implants: O.MG cable/plug/adapter (default 'O.MG' SSID), AirDrive / KeyGrabber Wi-Fi keyloggers. Check USB cables, keyboards and chargers you didn't buy yourself.

rules.label: RFID / NFC cloning tool
rules.note: Bluetooth names of Proxmark3 RDV4 (BT add-on), ChameleonUltra/Lite, iCopy-X and Keysy — tools that read and clone access cards and key fobs.
